opus-5.5.text:
I think wanting to be number one is actually a healthy instinct, as long as you're honest about what it means. For me it's never really been about beating a specific person or topping some leaderboard for a week. Leaderboards move fast. Somebody always comes along with a bigger model or more data, and if your whole sense of worth is tied to that, you'll burn out.

What I try to aim for is being number one in a direction, being the person or the team that saw something early and pushed it further than anyone else. When we worked on image synthesis and GANs years ago, a lot of people thought generating realistic images was a toy problem. We believed it would matter, so we kept pushing on quality, resolution, and control, and over time that became a real field. That kind of being first, where you open a door, is much more meaningful to me than winning a benchmark by half a point.

There's also a practical side. Research is competitive, especially now in AI, and the best people are all working on similar things. If you don't aim high, you end up doing incremental work that's forgotten in six months. So I do tell my team that we should try to build the best thing in the world for the problem we choose. But choosing the problem is the most important part. You want a problem that's important, that you have some unique advantage on, maybe data, compute, or insight, and that isn't crowded yet.

And finally, I think you need some humility. Even if you're number one today, the field will move past you. What lasts isn't the ranking, it's whether your work changed how people think, or whether others built on it. That's the version of number one I care about.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls work incremental when researchers do not aim high, but does not characterize scientific progress itself as incremental.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I used to care about that a lot. When I was a PhD student and then early in my career, I thought the goal was to beat everyone on the benchmark, to be the first name on the paper that everybody cites. And there is some value in that mindset, because it pushes you to work hard and not settle. But over time I realized that "number one" is a very narrow way to measure yourself, and it is also a moving target. The moment you are at the top of a leaderboard, someone else comes along a few months later and takes it. If that is the only thing that gives you meaning, you will never be satisfied.

What I think about more now is whether the problem itself matters. Are you working on something that, if it succeeds, actually changes how people build things or how a field moves forward? When I was doing generative models for images and video, for example, the question was never really "can we get a slightly better FID score." It was "can we make a model that people can actually use to create something they could not create before." That is a different kind of ambition. It is less about ranking and more about impact.

I also think being number one is often a team outcome, not an individual one. Almost everything I am proud of was done with a group of people where each person brought something I could not. So if I am being honest, the way I aim high today is to try to pick the right direction early, be willing to be wrong and change course, and surround myself with people who are better than me at the things I am not good at. If you do that consistently, sometimes you end up being first. But being first is a side effect, not the goal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts chasing slightly better benchmark scores with pursuing impact, but it does not characterize scientific progress as incremental.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by number one. Research is not a race where everyone runs on the same track. You choose the problems you work on, and that choice is a big part of your contribution.

For me, a more useful ambition is to do something that matters—to solve a problem that people couldn’t solve before, or to open up a direction that other people can build on. You should have high standards and understand the strongest work in your field. But if you’re constantly asking, “Am I ahead of this person?” it can distract you from asking, “Is this actually the right problem?”

So I would aim for work that is original and useful. If recognition follows, that’s great. But recognition shouldn’t be the thing that tells you what to work on.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes solving previously unsolved problems or opening new directions, but does not characterize scientific progress as incremental.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to be ambitious, but I would be careful about making “number one” the goal. Research is hard to rank on a single axis. You can publish more papers or do better on a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re asking the most important questions.

For me, the more useful ambition is to do something that matters—to solve a problem that people couldn’t solve before, or open up a direction that other researchers can build on. That gives you something concrete to work toward. You still need to know what the best people are doing, and you should hold yourself to a very high standard. But ultimately, I would rather ask, “What can I contribute?” than “Where do I rank?”

r001.rationale: The response discusses solving previously unsolved problems and opening new research directions, but does not characterize scientific progress as incremental.
